disclaimer: Rockstar has not published GTA 6 online requirements. Thresholds are derived from GTA Online guidance, comparable session-based titles and standard networking practice. Regional figures are typical wired best-case round trips, not guarantees. Nothing here is measured — the grade applies to numbers the caller supplies.

grading.note: Any failing axis caps the grade at C.

regions.label: North America — East
regions.note: Densest peering on the continent. Wired fibre players routinely see sub-20 ms to Rockstar services.

regions.label: North America — West
regions.note: Good local edges, but cross-country lobbies add 50–70 ms when matchmaking sends you east.

regions.label: Europe — West
regions.note: The best-connected region in this table. Anything above 40 ms here is your own line, not distance.

regions.label: Europe — Central & East
regions.note: Frankfurt carries most traffic; eastern ISPs sometimes route through it rather than peering locally.

regions.label: United Kingdom & Ireland
regions.note: Short hop to London, but older FTTC lines add interleaving delay that looks like distance.

regions.label: Latin America
regions.note: São Paulo is the regional hub. Traffic from Mexico and the Andes often exits to Miami first.

regions.label: Middle East & North Africa
regions.note: Gulf peering is strong; North African routes still transit Marseille, which costs 30–50 ms.

regions.label: India & South Asia
regions.note: Mumbai edges are excellent. Games without a local lobby push you to Singapore for ~65 ms.

regions.label: Southeast Asia
regions.note: Singapore serves the whole region, so Manila and Jakarta pay a submarine-cable tax of 20–40 ms.

regions.label: Australia & New Zealand
regions.note: Sydney is fine domestically; any US-hosted lobby is a hard 150 ms floor no router can fix.

regions.label: Japan & Korea
regions.note: Best-in-class domestic fibre. If your ping is high here, suspect the last hop inside your home.

connectionTypes.label: Fibre to the home (FTTP)
connectionTypes.note: The reference case. Latency is dominated by distance, not the access line.

connectionTypes.label: Cable / coax (DOCSIS)
connectionTypes.note: Shared upstream. Evenings in a busy node are where cable jitter shows up.

connectionTypes.label: DSL / VDSL / FTTC
connectionTypes.note: Interleaving adds a fixed penalty. Ask your ISP for fast-path or low-latency interleave.

connectionTypes.label: 5G home broadband
connectionTypes.note: Bandwidth is rarely the problem; the radio scheduler makes jitter the problem.

connectionTypes.label: Phone hotspot / mobile data
connectionTypes.note: Workable for downloads, hostile for lobbies. Expect NAT problems on top of jitter.

connectionTypes.label: Satellite (LEO or geostationary)
connectionTypes.note: LEO is playable at ~50 ms added; geostationary is not, at roughly 600 ms round trip.

devices.label: PC (Windows)
howToMeasure: Plug into Ethernet if you can, then close Steam, Rockstar Launcher, browsers and anything syncing.
Run a browser speed test on a server in your own region and write down download, upload and ping.
Open Command Prompt and run ping -n 50 1.1.1.1 — read the average for latency and the max-minus-min spread as your jitter.
In the same output, read the loss percentage. Anything above 0% on a wired line is a fault, not noise.
Repeat once in the evening peak. The peak number is the one that decides whether GTA Online feels good.
devices.caveat: Windows reports the path to a public DNS resolver, not to a Rockstar lobby, so treat the figure as a floor rather than an exact match.

devices.label: PlayStation 5
howToMeasure: Settings → Network → Connection Status → Test Internet Connection.
Record download, upload and NAT type. NAT Type 1 or 2 is fine; Type 3 will cause matchmaking failures.
The console does not report jitter or loss — take those from a PC or phone on the same network.
If you are on Wi-Fi, note the band: 5 GHz or 6 GHz only, never 2.4 GHz for online play.
devices.caveat: The PS5 test measures against Sony's servers and consistently reads lower than real-world game throughput.

devices.label: Xbox Series X|S
howToMeasure: Settings → General → Network settings → Test network speed & statistics.
Read download, upload, latency, packet loss and wireless strength — Xbox reports all of them.
Check the NAT line on the same screen: Open is what you want, Strict will break invites.
Re-run it once with a cable if the wireless figure disappoints. That single test settles most lag arguments.
devices.caveat: Xbox is the only platform that reports loss and latency natively, which makes it the best measuring device in the house.

devices.label: Cloud / handheld streaming
howToMeasure: Test on the exact device and network you will stream from, not on the desktop next to it.
Record ping and jitter first — streaming fails on latency long before it fails on bandwidth.
Confirm sustained download of at least 25 Mbps for 1080p60 and 40 Mbps for 4K.
Watch for a rising jitter number over a five-minute stream; that is a Wi-Fi problem, not an ISP problem.
devices.caveat: Streaming adds encode and decode latency on top of network latency, so a good network score is necessary but not sufficient.
